method: Official pages could not be opened from the research environment (network policy). Each summary was written in Clyntique's own words from search results that pointed to the official page, cross-checked against secondary summaries where available. No quotations and no dates are recorded; a policy admin adds them after reading the page.

version.title: Weight loss and cosmetic ads: adults only
version.summary: Meta only allows ads for weight loss or weight gain products and services, dietary and health supplements, and cosmetic products, procedures or surgeries when they target people aged 18 or over.
version.legalExplanation: Meta's health and wellness standard treats these products as restricted goods. Delivery to under-18s is not allowed.
version.remediationAction: Set the audience minimum age to 18 or over in the campaign and confirm it before submitting.
applicabilityConditions: The ad promotes weight loss or weight gain products or services, dietary or health supplements, or cosmetic products, procedures or surgeries.
exceptions: General wellbeing products and services, such as fitness services, fitness equipment and health clubs.
General food products, including protein products.
Non-permanent cosmetic and beauty products, such as creams, makeup, hair products and photo editing apps.
Dental products, such as teeth whitening.
version.reviewNote: Checked on 30 Oct 2026 against the live official page (signed out). The page states no effective or updated date, so no date is recorded. Scope extended to weight gain, supplements and cosmetic surgeries; exemptions taken from the page. Still a draft: a policy admin must verify it against the page and a different admin must approve it.

version.title: Weight loss and cosmetic ads: body image and claims
version.summary: Meta ads for weight loss or weight gain, or for cosmetic products or procedures, must not attack a person's appearance, body parts or hygiene. Weight loss or gain ads must not show close-ups of pinched fat, claim results from wearables alone, promise outcomes in a set time without qualification, or claim to cure listed incurable diseases.
version.legalExplanation: Meta's health and wellness standard restricts imagery and messages that create negative self-image.
version.remediationAction: Remove comparison and close-up body imagery; describe the service and its benefits without judging appearance.
applicabilityConditions: The ad promotes weight loss or weight gain products or services, or cosmetic products or procedures.
exceptions: With 18+ targeting, ads for cosmetic products, procedures or surgeries may show before-and-after transformations.
restrictedClaims: Negative statements attacking someone's appearance, body parts or hygiene
Close-up images of pinching fat (weight loss or gain)
Claims that results come solely from wearable products
Sensational claims or promised results within a set time without qualification
Claims to cure, heal or eliminate the incurable diseases Meta lists
version.reviewNote: Checked on 30 Oct 2026 against the live official page (signed out). The page states no effective or updated date, so no date is recorded. Corrected: the page restricts attacks on appearance and pinched-fat close-ups, and allows cosmetic before-and-after for adults; unsupported items moved to open questions. Still a draft: a policy admin must verify it against the page and a different admin must approve it.

version.title: Do not assert or imply a person's health condition
version.summary: Meta ads must not say or suggest that the viewer has a physical or mental health condition, or that the advertiser knows medical information about them or their family.
version.legalExplanation: Meta's personal attributes standard covers direct and indirect assertions about health, among other attributes. Second-person phrasing ("your acne") is a common trigger in practice; that point comes from secondary guides, not Meta's text.
version.remediationAction: Describe the treatment and who it is for in general terms ("treatment for acne") instead of addressing the viewer's condition.
exceptions: Public service announcements about health topics, as long as they don't assert that someone or their family has a health condition.
restrictedClaims: Direct or indirect statements that the viewer has a medical condition
Copy implying the advertiser knows the viewer's health information
version.reviewNote: Checked on 30 Oct 2026 against the live official page (signed out). The page states no effective or updated date, so no date is recorded. Confirmed; exception added from the page. Still a draft: a policy admin must verify it against the page and a different admin must approve it.

version.title: Prescription drugs and online prescribing need Google certification
version.summary: Google restricts ads for online prescribing, dispensing or selling prescription drugs, such as online pharmacies and telemedicine providers. Advertisers must apply to Google first, and prescription drug terms are restricted in ads, landing pages and keywords; depending on the location they may be allowed.
version.legalExplanation: Google's healthcare and medicines policy sets country-by-country rules and certification. Certified ads may show as 'Eligible (limited)'.
version.remediationAction: Remove prescription drug terms, or confirm the clinic holds Google certification for each targeted country before running the ad.
applicabilityConditions: The ad or landing page mentions prescription medicines or offers prescribing, for example injectables or weight loss medicines.
restrictedClaims: Prescription drug names or terms in ad text, keywords or landing pages without certification
substantiationRequirements: Google certification for the advertiser's domain in each targeted country
version.reviewNote: Checked on 30 Oct 2026 against the live official page (signed out). The page states no effective or updated date, so no date is recorded. Confirmed except the country rows, which still need a person to select United States and United Arab Emirates on the page. Still a draft: a policy admin must verify it against the page and a different admin must approve it.

version.title: Health is a sensitive category for personalized ads
version.summary: Google does not allow advertiser-built audiences (for example remarketing or customer lists) to target people based on health conditions, treatments or procedures.
version.legalExplanation: Google's personalized advertising policy treats health as a personal hardship category: ads should not target people in ways that exploit their difficulties.
version.remediationAction: Use contextual or Google's own predefined audiences; remove remarketing or customer-list targeting tied to treatments or conditions.
applicabilityConditions: The campaign uses advertiser-curated audiences (for example remarketing or customer lists) for health conditions, treatments for chronic conditions, or invasive procedures such as cosmetic surgery or injections.
exceptions: Google's predefined audiences may be used.
version.reviewNote: Checked on 30 Oct 2026 against the live official page (signed out). The page states no effective or updated date, so no date is recorded. Confirmed; applicability taken from the page. Still a draft: a policy admin must verify it against the page and a different admin must approve it.

version.title: TikTok healthcare ads must meet each market's rules
version.summary: TikTok allows ads for medical institutions, pharmacies and over-the-counter medicines only where the market's requirements are met, usually proof of approval or certification from the local regulator and an audience aged 18 or over. Prescription medicines are not allowed in the markets the policy lists.
version.legalExplanation: TikTok's healthcare and pharmaceuticals policy defers to local healthcare advertising law and lists requirements per market.
version.remediationAction: Check the market row for the targeted country, keep the clinic's licence or approval ready for TikTok review and set the audience to 18 or over.
restrictedClaims: Prescription medicine promotion
substantiationRequirements: Proof of local regulator approval or licence, where the market table requires it

version.title: TikTok weight loss claims: no exaggeration, adults only
version.summary: TikTok ads and landing pages must not make exaggerated or harmful weight loss or muscle gain claims. Weight loss claims must be shown only to people aged 18 or over and framed around a healthy lifestyle. Some products, such as weight loss surgery or supplements, are allowed only in some countries.
version.legalExplanation: TikTok's weight management and body image policy covers both the ad and its landing page.
version.remediationAction: Remove exaggerated results, target 18 or over, and present the service as part of a healthy lifestyle.
restrictedClaims: Exaggerated or harmful weight loss or muscle gain claims

version.title: TikTok cosmetic surgery ads in the United States
version.summary: TikTok's North America update allows ads for cosmetic surgery and related aesthetic procedures under conditions: working with a TikTok sales representative, an adult audience and licensed providers. Ads must disclose medical risks and recovery time and must not use before-and-after images that exaggerate results.
version.legalExplanation: This comes from a TikTok policy update notice, not the main policy page. It may change again.
version.remediationAction: Confirm eligibility with the TikTok representative, add risk and recovery information, and remove exaggerated before-and-after images.
restrictedClaims: Before-and-after images that exaggerate results
Body shaming
Unsafe health claims
substantiationRequirements: Disclosure of risks and recovery time

version.title: Endorsements and testimonials (US)
version.summary: Endorsements and patient testimonials must reflect honest experiences, and any material connection (payment, free treatment, employment) must be clearly disclosed. Advertisers are responsible for their endorsers and should guide and monitor them. A testimonial about results implies they are typical unless the advertiser can show otherwise or clearly states what results people can generally expect.
version.legalExplanation: The FTC revised the Endorsement Guides in 2023. The Guides are advisory, but practices inconsistent with them can lead to FTC action under Section 5.
version.remediationAction: Disclose material connections clearly, keep records of endorser guidance, and add a generally expected results statement or remove atypical results.
restrictedClaims: Testimonials presenting exceptional results as typical
Undisclosed paid or incentivised endorsements
substantiationRequirements: Evidence that the results shown are representative, or a clear statement of generally expected results

version.title: Health claims need competent and reliable scientific evidence (US)
version.summary: Health benefit and safety claims must be backed by competent and reliable scientific evidence before the ad runs, generally well-designed human clinical trials. Anecdotes, animal or lab studies and weak qualifiers such as "may help" do not make an unsupported claim acceptable.
version.legalExplanation: The FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance applies to health claims across product and service types. These points come from law firm summaries; read the guidance itself.
version.remediationAction: Ask the client for the study behind each health claim, or reword the claim to what the evidence supports.
restrictedClaims: Efficacy or safety claims without supporting human clinical evidence
Claims of scientific consensus without evidence of consensus
substantiationRequirements: Competent and reliable scientific evidence, generally randomized controlled human trials, matching the claim

version.title: UAE health ads need health authority approval before publishing
version.summary: In the UAE, health advertisements, including social media posts by clinics, need approval and a licence from the Ministry of Health and Prevention before they are published. Content must be truthful, balanced and not misleading. Approval does not replace requirements from other authorities, such as emirate health regulators.
version.legalExplanation: MOHAP's guidelines describe the approval request. Legal summaries cite older resolutions; confirm the current legal basis with counsel.
version.remediationAction: Get the advertisement approval reference from the client before submitting, and confirm whether DHA or DOH approval is also needed for the emirate.
restrictedClaims: Publishing a health advertisement without health authority approval
Misleading or unbalanced health statements
substantiationRequirements: Health advertisement approval or licence reference for the ad
